title: Specific latent heat of fusion and vaporization
topicTitle: Specific latent heat of fusion and vaporization
notes: Specific latent heat L is the heat absorbed or released when 1 kg of a substance changes state at constant temperature. The heat is Q = m L, and there is no Δθ term while the change of state is going on.
The specific latent heat of fusion, L_f, is for melting or freezing. For ice at 0°C it is about 3.34 × 10^5 J/kg. Melting absorbs this heat. Freezing releases it.

The specific latent heat of vaporization, L_v, is for boiling or condensation. For water at 100°C it is about 2.26 × 10^6 J/kg, several times larger than L_f, because the molecules must be separated much further.

During melting the temperature stays at the melting point until all the solid has changed. The supplied energy increases the potential energy of the molecules, not the average kinetic energy that temperature tracks.
A warming problem that crosses a change of state is done in pieces: mc Δθ up to the change point, then m L, then mc Δθ in the new state. Leaving out m L is the usual error.
The same L applies to the reverse change. Condensing 1 kg of steam at 100°C releases m L_v, which is why a steam burn is severe compared with a burn from water at the same temperature.

summary: Specific latent heat is the heat per unit mass for a change of state at constant temperature, Q = m L. Fusion covers melting and freezing. Vaporization covers boiling and condensation. A path that both changes state and changes temperature needs an m L term and an mc Δθ term.
